{{Short description|Argentine molecular biologist}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2024}}
[[File:Alberto Kornblihtt en el stand de CONICET 1.jpg|thumb|Kornblihtt at CONICET]]
'''Alberto Kornblihtt''' (born June 30, 1954) is an Argentine molecular biologist who specializes in alternative [[RiboNucleic Acid|ribonucleic acid]] splicing.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Viegas |first=J |date=2015 |title=Profile of Alberto Kornblihtt |url= |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=112 |issue=7 |pages=1917–1918 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1421075111 |pmid=25425664 |pmc=4343084 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.1917V |doi-access=free}}</ref> During his postdoctoral training with Francisco Baralle in Oxford, Kornblihtt documented one of the first cases of alternative splicing, explaining how a single [[Transcription (biology)|transcribed gene]] can generate multiple protein variants. Kornblihtt was elected as a foreign associate of the [[National Academy of Sciences of the United States]] in 2011, received the Diamond Award for the most relevant scientist of Argentina of the decade, alongside physicist [[Juan Martín Maldacena|Juan Martin Maldacena]], in 2013,<ref name=":0" /> and was incorporated to the Académie des Sciences of France in 2022.

== Personal life ==
Kornblihtt is married, with two adult sons. Outside of his research, Kornblihtt appreciates the opportunity to teach undergraduate biology students at the [[University of Buenos Aires]]. In his free time, Kornblihtt enjoys cooking, classical music, numerous genres of literature, etymology, and is a life-long lover of cinema.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Casadio |first=M |date=2017 |title=Alberto Kornblihtt: Coupling alternative splicing with transcription |journal=Journal of Cell Biology |volume=216 |issue=2 |pages=284–285 |doi=10.1083/jcb.201701050 |pmid=28104749 |pmc=5294796 |s2cid=29616524 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Alberto Kornblihtt was born on June 30, 1954, in Buenos Aires, Argentina.<ref name=":0" /> His parents taught mathematics and geography, providing Kornblihtt and his two siblings, who also pursued careers in science and education, with an environment for knowledge and learning at an early age. When he was 16 years old, Kornblihtt enrolled in a high school botany and biology class instructed by Rosa Guaglianone, allowing Kornblihtt the opportunity to perform laboratory and microscopy work. This experience launched Kornblihtt's interest in DNA and mRNA. Following high school, Kornblihtt continued his education at the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales (School of Sciences) of the [[University of Buenos Aires]], earning a Biology degree in 1977. In 1980, Kornblihtt went on to earn his PhD in biochemistry from Campomar Foundation in Buenos Aires, under the mentorship of Héctor Torres. Kornblihtt then relocated to [[University of Oxford|Oxford]], where he held a postdoctoral position from 1981 through 1984 at the [[Sir William Dunn School of Pathology]]. Kornblihtt worked with Professor Francisco Barralle during his postdoctoral research, and together, they were successful in [[Cloning vector|cloning]] the human fibronectin gene.<ref name=":0" /> They determined that [[fibronectin]], an important [[glycoprotein]] for [[cell adhesion]] and tissue repair,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yamada |first=K. M. |date=2000 |title=Fibronectin peptides in cell migration and wound repair |url= |journal=The Journal of Clinical Investigation |volume=105 |issue=11 |pages=1507–1509 |doi=10.1172/JCI10119 |pmid=10841505 |pmc=300861}}</ref> was alternatively spliced and could result in the generation of twenty polypeptides.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kornblihtt |first1=Alberto |last2=Umezawa |first2=K |last3=Vibe-Pederson |first3=K |last4=Baralle |first4=F.E. |date=1985 |title=Primary structure of human fibronectin: differential splicing may generate at least 10 polypeptides from a single gene |journal=The EMBO Journal |volume=4 |issue=7 |pages=1755–1759 |doi=10.1002/j.1460-2075.1985.tb03847.x |pmid=2992939 |pmc=554414}}</ref>

== Research ==
After completing his postdoctoral research in Oxford, Kornblihtt returned to Argentina in 1984 and accepted a position as an assistant professor of molecular and cell biology at Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales at the University of Buenos Aires. In 1991 he was appointed full professor and at present he is professor emeritus. Kornblihtt is also a senior [[National Scientific and Technical Research Council|CONICET]] investigator of the CONICET and works with a research team to study the regulation of alternative ribonucleic acid splicing. [[Alternative splicing]] occurs during [[gene expression]], allowing exons from a gene to be excluded or included, resulting in a single gene generating multiple proteins. Major projects in Kornblihtt's lab focus on: 1) [[Coupling]] transcription with alternative splicing; 2) Alternative splicing and Chromatin; 3) Alternative splicing and spinal muscular atrophy; 4) Ultraviolet light irradiation and alternative splicing; and 5) Alternative splicing in plants.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Regulation of Alternative Splicing |url=http://ark.fbmc.fcen.uba.ar/home_eng.php |access-date=March 5, 2021 |website=The Kornblihtt Lab}}</ref>

== Research on coupling transcription with alternative splicing ==
Kornblihtt's lab focuses on the mechanisms that couple [[Transcription (biology)|transcription]] with alternative splicing for the regulation of [[alternative pre-mRNA splicing]]. [[Transcription (biology)|Transcription]] is the process in which a genetic sequence of a gene is transcribed, or changed, from [[Central dogma of molecular biology|DNA into RNA]], to allow for protein production.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rabiya |date=October 5, 2019 |title=DNA Transcription: Definition, Stages, & Diagram |url=https://ibiologia.com/dna-transcription/ |access-date=March 6, 2021 |website=IBiologia}}</ref> One of the most significant accomplishments in Kornblihtt's research came in 1997. Kornblihtt's research team was able to an alternative splicing assay combined with promoter swapping to demonstrate that transcription promoters affect the outcome of splicing <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cramer |first=P |date=1997 |title=Functional association between promoter structure and transcript alternative splicing |url= |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=94 |issue=21 |pages=11456–11460 |doi=10.1073/pnas.94.21.11456 |pmid=9326631 |pmc=23504 |bibcode=1997PNAS...9411456C |doi-access=free}}</ref> They later determined that the coupling of transcription and splicing is dependent upon transcriptional elongation speed, or kinetic coupling, and the impact of transcribing [[RNA polymerase II]] on splicing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kornblihtt |first1=Alberto |last2=de la Mata |first2=Manuel |last3=Alonso |first3=Claudio |last4=Kadener |first4=Sebastián |last5=Bentley |first5=David |last6=Cramer |first6=Paula |title=A slow RNA polymerase II affects alternative splicing in vivo |journal=Molecular Cell |year=2003 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=525–532 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2003.08.001 |pmid=14536091 |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.12110/paper_10972765_v12_n2_p525_DeLaMata |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alló |first1=Mariano |last2=Buggiano |first2=Valeria |last3=Fededa |first3=Juan |last4=Petrillo |first4=Ezequiel |last5=Schor |first5=Ignacio |last6=de la Mata |first6=Manuel |last7=Agirre |first7=Eneritz |last8=Plass |first8=Mireya |last9=Eyras |first9=Eduardo |last10=Abou Elela |first10=Sherif |last11=Kornblihtt |first11=Alberto |title=Control of alternative splicing through siRNA-mediated transcriptional gene silencing |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/nsmb.1620 |journal=Nature Structural & affects alternative splicing events, with slow elongation increasing inclusion of approximately 80% of [[exon]]s and skipping of approximately 20% in mammalian cells.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite === More on alternative splicing and chromatin ===
An additional area of Kornblihtt's study investigated the impact of [[chromatin]] structure on alternative splicing. Kornblihtt's research team demonstrated that alternative splicing is impacted by chromatin structure and the rate of transcription.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schor |first=I. E. |date=2009 |title=Neuronal cell depolarization induces intragenic chromatin modifications affecting NCAM alternative splicing |url= |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=106 |issue=11 |pages=4325–4330 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0810666106 |pmid=19251664 |pmc=2657401 |bibcode=2009PNAS..106.4325S |doi-access=free}}</ref> They found that a tighter chromatin structure provides lower rates of elongation and looser chromatin structures provide a higher rate of elongation of transcription.<ref name=":2" /> These studies further contributed to the relationship between alternative splicing and epigenetics, which Kornblihtt's team used in studying potential therapies for Skeletal Muscular Atrophy.

=== Research on alternative splicing and spinal muscular atrophy ===
[[Spinal muscular atrophy|Spinal Muscular Atrophy]] (SMA) is a hereditary [[degenerative disease]] of the [[Central nervous system disease|central nervous system]] resulting from a spinal motor neuron (SMN) protein shortage.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=About SMA |url=https://www.spinraza.com/en_us/home/what-is-sma/about-sma.html |access-date=March 7, 2021 |website=Spinraza}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cartegni |first1=Luca |last2=Hastings |first2=Michelle |last3=Calarco |first3=John |last4=de Stanchina |first4=Elisa |last5=Krainer |first5=Adrian |title=Determinants of Exon 7 Splicing in the Spinal Muscular Atrophy Genes, SMN1 and SMN2 |journal=American Journal of Human Genetics |year=2006 |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=63–77 |doi=10.1086/498853 |pmid=16385450 |pmc=1380224}}</ref> This is due to the deletion or mutation of Survival of Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1). Due to the faulty SMN1 gene, SMA patients do not have enough SMN protein. SMA patients must depend on Survivor of Motor Neurons 2 (SMN2), a gene that all humans have. SMN2 cannot produce sufficient full-length protein for the motor neurons to signal muscles due to sequence differences and the exclusion of exon 7, resulting in the overall SMN protein deficiency.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> As a treatment strategy for SMA, the first FDA-approved drug, known as [[Nusinersen|Spinraza]] was developed by Dr. [[Adrian R. Krainer|Adrian Krainer]] and his [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]] colleagues.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Krainer |first=Adrian |date=October 23, 2019 |title=Adrian Krainer elected to National Academy of Medicine |url=https://www.cshl.edu/adrian-krainer-elected-to-national-academy-of-medicine/ |access-date=March 7, 2021 |website=Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory}}</ref> [[Nusinersen|Spinraza]] is an [[oligonucleotide]] that works to activate SMN2 to make more SMN protein in SMA patients.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chen |first=Inês |date=November 19, 2019 |title=An antisense oligonucleotide splicing modulator to treat spinal muscular atrophy |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d42859-019-00090-4 |access-date=March 7, 2021 |journal=Nature Portfolio}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marasco |first=Luciano |date=November 2019 |title=El splicing alternativo y la cura de la atrofia muscular espinal |url=https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/handle/11336/123459 |journal=Conicet |volume=79 |pages=582–586}}</ref> In 2015, the families of Spinal Muscular Atrophy patients encouraged Kornblihtt and Krainer to work together to improve the effectiveness of [[Nusinersen|Spinraza]] or to develop alternative therapies to be used in conjunction with [[Nusinersen|Spinraza]]. Kornblihtt's research team focuses on epigenetic strategies, a different mechanism than used [[Nusinersen|Spinraza]], to increase SMN protein from the SMN2 gene.<ref>{{Cite web |last=de Barros |first=Ana |date=May 30, 2017 |title=Argentinian Receives Cure SMA Award to Research SMA Epigenetics |url=https://smanewstoday.com/news-posts/2017/05/30/140k-award-kornblihtt-sma-study-epigenetics/ |access-date=March 7, 2021 |website=SMA News Today}}</ref> Epigenetics studies changes in gene expression, without alteration to the DNA sequence.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Elnitski |first=Laura |title=Epigenetics |url=https://smanewstoday.com/news-posts/2017/05/30/140k-award-kornblihtt-sma-study-epigenetics/ |access-date=March 7, 2021}}</ref> In 2017 and 2019, Kornblihtt received three separate grants from CURE SMA and FAME (Families of SMA, Argentina) to support continued work on his projects "Epigenetics in ''SMN2'' E7 Alternative Splicing" and "Epigenetics in SMN2 E7 Alternative Splicing II".<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=March 28, 2019 |title=Cure SMA Awards $200,000 Grant to Alberto Kornblihtt, PhD |url=https://www.curesma.org/cure-sma-awards-200000-grant-to-alberto-kornblihtt-phd-universidad-de-buenos-aires/ |access-date=March 5, 2021 |website=CureSMA}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=May 15, 2017 |title=Cure SMA Awards $140,000 Grant to Alberto Kornblihtt, PhD, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Argentina |url=https://www.curesma.org/cure-sma-awards-140000-grant-to-alberto-kornblihtt-phd-universidad-de-buenos-aires-argentina/ |access-date=March 5, 2021 |website=Cure SMA}}</ref> In these projects, Kornblihtt's team has worked on the regulation of alternative pre-mRNA splicing to develop new mechanisms for SMN protein development, using a single gene to generate multiple proteins.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":6" /> Kornblihtt's lab continues to work on the SMN2 gene for SMA therapy that focus specifically on exon 7 inclusion to work in conjunction with oligonucleotide treatments, such as [[Nusinersen|Spinraza]].<ref name=":4" />

== Other research ==

=== UV-induced DNA damage ===
As a continuation of their longterm research on alternative splicing, Kornblihtt's team also studied the impact [[DNA damage|DNA damage induced by Ultraviolet light]] (UV) irradiation on alternative splicing in human skin cells. Their research demonstrated that the DNA-damage response to sunlight causes [[Protein phosphorylation|phosphorylation]] of the RNA polymerase and slowing of the enzyme. Through their research, they found that UV irradiation is necessary to trigger the alternative splicing of many genes and promoting the death of damaged or mutated cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Viegas |first=Jennifer |date=February 17, 2015 |title=Profile of Alberto Kornblihtt |journal=PNAS |volume=112 |issue=7 |pages=1917–1918 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1421075111 |pmid=25425664 |pmc=4343084 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.1917V |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Alternative splicing in plants ===
Adding to their research performed on human cells, Kornblihtt's team expanded their research to study transcription and alternative splicing in plants. The plant [[Arabidopsis thaliana]] was used to investigate how external lighting conditions affected alternative splicing. Research showed that the chloroplast, where photosynthesis occurs, senses light and sends a signal to the cell nucleus to regulate alternative splicing.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Kornblihtt |first1=Alberto |last2=Godoy Herz |first2=Micaela |date=March 26, 2019 |title=Alternative Splicing and Transcription Elongation in Plants |journal=Frontiers in Plant Science |volume=73 |pages=1066–1074 |doi=10.3389/fpls.2019.00309 |pmid=30972082 |pmc=6443983 |doi-access=free}}</ref> As previously found in mammalian cells, Kornblihtt's team demonstrated that alternative splicing in plants responds to the [[Coupling|kinetic coupling mechanism]]. Their research further showed that light promotes elongation in RNA polymerase II (Pol II) while elongation is lowered in darkness.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Godoy Herz |first1=Micaela |last2=Kubaczka |first2=Guillermina |last3=Brzyżek |first3=Grzegorz |last4=Swiezewski |first4=Szymon |last5=Petrillo |first5=Ezequiel |last6=Kornblihtt |first6=Alberto |date=January 17, 2019 |title=Light Regulates Plant Alternative Splicing through the Control of Transcriptional Elongation |journal=Molecular Cell |volume=73 |issue=5 |pages=1066–1074 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2018.12.005 |pmid=30661982 |doi-access=free|hdl=11336/123464 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
* In 1991, Kornblihtt received the Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship in Natural Sciences, awarded on the basis of previous achievement and basis of prior achievement and outstanding promise.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 8, 2020 |title=Current Fellows |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/current/ |url-status=dead |access-date=March 8, 2021 |website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402183317/http://www.gf.org/fellows/current?page=3}}</ref>
* Between 2002 and 2017, Kornblihtt received the International Research Scholar of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] (HHMI) Award, given to scientists outside of the United States who have notably contributed to biological science research.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=October 2, 2012 |title=Howard Hughes Medical Institute Announces Senior International Research Scholars |url=https://philanthropynewsdigest.org/news/howard-hughes-medical-institute-announces-senior-international-research-scholars |access-date=March 8, 2021 |website=Philanthropy News Digest}}</ref>
* In 2003 and 2013, Kornblihtt was the recipient of the [[Konex Award|Konex]] Platinum Award, a cultural award given to Argentines in different fields of work.<ref name=":2" />
* From 2000 through 2008, Kornblihtt was awarded as a chair from the Fundacion Antorchas.<ref name=":2" />
* In 2010, Kornblihtt was the recipient of the Bicentennial Medal.<ref name=":2" />
* In 2010, Kornblihtt was elected as Investigator of the Argentine Nation Prize, granted by the President of Argentina.<ref name=":2" />
* From 2010 – 2011, Kornblihtt served as the President of the Argentine Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (SAIB).<ref name=":2" />
* From 2010 – 2015, Kornblihtt served as a member of the Board of Reviewing Editors of Science.<ref name=":3" />
* In 2011, Kornblihtt received Honorary Mention, Domingo Faustino Sarmiento of the Argentine Senate.<ref name=":2" />
* In 2011, Kornblihtt was elected as a Foreign Associate of the [[National Academy of Sciences of the United States|National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]<ref name=":3" />
* In 2012, Kornblihtt was awarded the [[The World Academy of Sciences|TWAS]] prize in Medical Sciences, an award given to individual scientists in developing countries for outstanding scientific contributions.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=TWAS Awards |url=https://twas.org/opportunity/twas-awards |access-date=March 8, 2021 |website=United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization}}</ref>
* In 2012, Kornblihtt was elected foreign member of EMBO (European Molecular Biology Organization).
* In 2013, Kornblihtt was a recipient of the Diamond Award for the most relevant scientist of Argentina of the decade, alongside physicist [[Juan Martín Maldacena|Juan Martin Maldacena]].<ref name=":0" />
* In 2022, Kornblihtt was elected as foreign member of the Académie de Sciences of France.
* Kornblihitt is a three-time recipient of the CURE SMA and FAME Grant in 2017, 2019 and 2023 for his research projects, Epigenetics in ''SMN2'' E7 Alternative Splicing" and "Epigenetics in SMN2 E7 Alternative Splicing II".<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":6" />
